title: Hurricane Helene (2024)
section: Synoptic Evolution: The Giant Wind Machine
text:
Synoptic Evolution: The Giant Wind Machine
On September 26, 2024, Hurricane Helene exploded into a massive Category 4 hurricane with 140 mph peak winds as it accelerated northward through the eastern Gulf. Helene’s tropical storm-force wind field spanned an incredible 400+ miles across, making it one of the largest hurricanes ever observed in the Gulf of Mexico.
Even though Helene’s eye tracked over 100 miles west of Tampa Bay, its enormous circulation acted as a colossal atmospheric piston, driving millions of tons of Gulf seawater straight into Tampa Bay.

title: Hurricane Helene (2024)
text:
Meteorological Telemetry at KTPA
KTPA’s sensors documented the most catastrophic coastal surge event in modern Tampa Bay history:

Catastrophic 6 to 7 Foot Storm Surge: Pushed by persistent gale-force southwesterly winds across the wide mouth of Tampa Bay, tide gauges shattered all-time records. The surge reached 6.5 to 7.2 feet above normal high tide, inundating thousands of homes across South Tampa, St. Petersburg, Treasure Island, and Clearwater Beach.
Sharp Barometric Collapse: Despite the storm’s center being over 100 miles away, station pressure at KTPA plummeted to 29.32 inHg (992.9 hPa) on the evening of September 26.
High Sustained Tropical Gales: Sustained winds reached 39 mph with gusts to 55 mph, knocking down electrical infrastructure throughout the coastal zone.

title: Hurricane Irma (2017)
text:
Synoptic Evolution & Closest Approach
Hurricane Irma was one of the most powerful Atlantic hurricanes on record, maintaining Category 5 intensity for three consecutive days with peak winds of 185 mph across the Caribbean. After making landfall in the Florida Keys as a Category 4 hurricane on September 10, Irma tracked northward up the interior spine of the Florida peninsula, passing just 25 miles east of Tampa during the pre-dawn hours of September 11.
The system’s close eastern transit placed Tampa Bay squarely in the storm’s powerful northwestern eyewall quadrant, subjecting the region to intense wind forces and an unprecedented barometric collapse.

title: Hurricane Irma (2017)
text:
Meteorological Telemetry at KTPA
Telemetry recorded at Tampa International Airport captured the single most violent pressure fluctuation in the station’s modern digital record:

Decade-Record Low Barometer: Station pressure plummeted from 29.95 inHg down to an astonishing 28.69 inHg (971.5 hPa) at 2:00 AM on September 11 as the eyewall skirted Polk and eastern Hillsborough counties.
The “Negative Surge” Phenomenon: Because Irma tracked east of Tampa, its counterclockwise circulation drove strong winds out of the northeast and east. Instead of pushing Gulf water into Tampa Bay, these offshore winds blew water out of Hillsborough Bay and Old Tampa Bay, draining the seabed and exposing mudflats for miles.
High-Velocity Wind Damage: Sustained winds peaked at 41 to 46 mph with violent squall gusts recorded up to 66 mph, snapping mature oak canopies and leaving over 70% of the metropolitan area without electrical power.

title: Christmas Arctic Freeze (2022)
section: Synoptic Evolution: The Christmas Polar Bomb
text:
Synoptic Evolution: The Christmas Polar Bomb
Just three months after Hurricane Ian, a historic continental polar vortex plunged southeast from the Canadian Arctic across the United States. On December 23, 2022, an intense arctic cold front raced through peninsular Florida, collapsing subtropical warmth in a matter of hours.
Behind the front, dense high pressure (30.34 inHg) locked in place, funneling howling arctic winds directly across Hillsborough and Pinellas counties over Christmas Eve and Christmas Day.

title: Christmas Arctic Freeze (2022)
text:
Meteorological Telemetry at KTPA
KTPA’s automated sensors chronicled one of the sharpest non-tropical weather anomalies in modern Tampa history:

All-Time Decade Record Low: On the morning of December 24, the thermometer plummeted to 29.0°F (-1.7°C)—the coldest temperature recorded in the entire 10-year archive (2015–2024).
Brutal Wind Chills: Strong north winds averaging 15 to 18 mph produced dangerous wind chills dipping into the upper teens (18°F), forcing the National Weather Service to issue rare Wind Chill Advisories for the Tampa metropolitan area.
Agricultural Hard Freeze: Sub-freezing temperatures persisted for over 8 consecutive hours, requiring regional citrus growers and strawberry farmers in Plant City to continuously spray water onto crops to form protective ice shields.

title: About the Project & Author
section: The Spark: A Lifelong Fascination with Weather
text:
The Spark: A Lifelong Fascination with Weather
Ever since I was little, my parents would constantly find me sitting in front of the TV, completely captivated by weather reports. While other kids were watching cartoons, I was drawn to the radar loops, the satellite views, and the meteorologists tracking cold fronts, squall lines, and tropical systems.
That fascination naturally followed me into the classroom. Throughout science classes in late elementary and early middle school, I was always asking why—trying to understand what drove high and low pressure, what created thunderstorms, and how the atmosphere operated. Outside of class, I dove into independent research and study, reading whatever I could find about atmospheric science and meteorology.
When the opportunity came to build this final project as a Junior at New College of Florida, choosing Tampa Bay’s weather was a natural extension of a lifelong passion that started in my childhood living room.

title: About the Project & Author
text:
Data & Methods

Primary Historical Dataset: 10 years (2015–2024) of hourly surface meteorological records from the automated station at Tampa International Airport (KTPA), sourced via NOAA’s National Centers for Environmental Information (NCEI) Local Climatological Data (LCD).
Real-Time Data: Live telemetry fetched dynamically from the National Weather Service (NWS) API.
Technology Stack: Built using R, Quarto, and the tidyverse (dplyr, ggplot2, patchwork, plotly, leaflet).

title: Hurricane Milton (2024)
text:
Synoptic Evolution: The Direct Hit
Just twelve days after Hurricane Helene devastated Tampa’s coastlines, Hurricane Milton formed in the southwestern Gulf and underwent one of the fastest explosive intensifications in world history, dropping to 897 hPa with 180 mph winds as a Category 5 superstorm.
Milton made landfall on the evening of October 9, 2024 near Siesta Key / Sarasota as a Category 3 hurricane. Because Milton made landfall immediately south of Tampa Bay, its northern eyewall—the most dangerous portion of the storm—slammed directly across St. Petersburg, Clearwater, Tampa, and KTPA.

title: Hurricane Milton (2024)
text:
Meteorological Telemetry at KTPA
Milton subjected Tampa Bay to simultaneous extreme rainfall and destructive eyewall winds:

Historic 16.03-Inch Deluge: The northern eyewall stalled over northern Pinellas and Hillsborough counties, dumping 16.03 inches of rain at KTPA in under 24 hours. This caused catastrophic flash flooding that submerged neighborhoods miles inland.
Eyewall Barometric Depression: Station pressure plummeted to 29.18 inHg (988.2 hPa) as the eyewall passed directly over the station.
Destructive Wind Force: Extreme hurricane-force gusts shredded trees, flattened power grids across the entire region, and famously shredded the fiberglass roof of Tropicana Field in downtown St. Petersburg.

title: Hurricane Michael (2018)
text:
Synoptic Evolution & Gulf Transit
In early October 2018, Hurricane Michael underwent explosive rapid intensification over the warm waters of the eastern Gulf of Mexico, deepening into an historic Category 5 hurricane with 160 mph sustained winds before devastating Mexico Beach and the Florida Panhandle.
While Michael’s center remained 200 miles west of Tampa as it rocketed north toward the Panhandle, its enormous wind field and intense low pressure exerted a profound hydrodynamic impact on Tampa Bay’s coastal waters.

title: Hurricane Michael (2018)
text:
Meteorological Telemetry at KTPA
Despite Michael’s core remaining far offshore, KTPA’s automated sensors clearly chronicled the cyclone’s passage:

Broad Pressure Deficit: Station pressure dipped to 29.75 inHg on October 10 as Michael reached peak Category 5 intensity off the Florida coast.
Reverse Negative Storm Surge: As Michael churned to the west, its counterclockwise winds drove steady northeasterly and easterly breezes across Tampa Bay. This continuous offshore gale pushed bay water toward the Gulf, lowering water levels across Hillsborough Bay by 2 to 2.5 feet below normal astronomical tide.
Dry Slotting: Unlike Hermine or Debby, Tampa Bay found itself in a continental dry slot behind Michael’s eastern rainbands, holding storm rainfall to just 0.50 inches at KTPA.

title: Hurricane Ian (2022)
text:
Synoptic Evolution & Last-Minute Track Shift
In late September 2022, Hurricane Ian intensified into a monstrous high-end Category 4/5 cyclone over the southeastern Gulf. Initial NHC forecast tracks pointed toward a catastrophic worst-case direct landfall inside Tampa Bay, triggering mandatory evacuations of over 300,000 residents across Hillsborough and Pinellas counties.
On the morning of September 28, Ian executed an eastward turn, making landfall 85 miles south at Cayo Costa / Fort Myers with 150+ mph winds. While Tampa Bay was spared a catastrophic direct surge, the southern landfall track created a historic meteorological phenomenon.

title: Hurricane Ian (2022)
text:
Meteorological Telemetry at KTPA
Because Ian made landfall to the south, Tampa Bay sat squarely on the cold, offshore northern quadrant of the storm:

Extreme Negative Surge: Northerly and northeasterly winds blowing between 30 and 45 mph literally siphoned water out of Tampa Bay, lowering water levels to 5.5 feet below normal. Hillsborough Bay, Bayshore Boulevard, and Davis Island basins became barren mudflats where residents famously walked on the dry bay floor.
Pressure Drop: Station pressure dropped to 29.56 inHg at KTPA on the evening of September 28 as Ian crossed the southern peninsula.
Spared Catastrophic Deluge: Because Ian’s core rain shield drifted across central and southern Florida, KTPA received 1.83 inches of rain, escaping the 15–20 inch deluges recorded just miles to the south in Sarasota and Lee counties.

title: Hurricane Hermine (2016)
text:
Synoptic Evolution & Storm Track
In late August 2016, Tropical Storm Hermine formed in the south-central Gulf of Mexico after traversing Cuba. As it curled northeast toward Florida’s Big Bend, it strengthened into a Category 1 hurricane with 80 mph peak winds. When Hermine made landfall near St. Marks, Florida on September 2, 2016, it officially ended Florida’s unprecedented 11-year streak without a hurricane landfall, stretching back to Hurricane Wilma in October 2005.
Although Hermine’s core tracked roughly 175 miles north-northwest of Tampa Bay, the storm’s extensive south and east quadrants swept broad spiral feeder bands across Hillsborough and Pinellas counties over three consecutive days.

title: Hurricane Hermine (2016)
text:
Meteorological Telemetry at KTPA
At Tampa International Airport, automated sensors recorded a steady descent in atmospheric pressure beginning on August 31, reaching a minimum of 29.77 inHg as the cyclone pushed into the northeastern Gulf. As the pressure bottomed out:

Persistent Tropical Gales: Sustained winds held between 20 and 30 mph for nearly 36 hours, punctuated by squall gusts exceeding 40 mph.
Prolonged Tropical Deluge: Outer feeder bands repeatedly trained over the Tampa metropolitan area, depositing 6.67 inches of rain over the 72-hour period.
Onshore Surge Inundation: Because Hermine’s counterclockwise circulation pushed sustained southwesterly and westerly winds across the mouth of Tampa Bay, water piled up into Hillsborough and Old Tampa Bay, producing 2 to 3 feet of storm surge that flooded coastal roads and submerged portions of Bayshore Boulevard.

title: Records
section: Detailed Profiles of Each Record Extreme
text:
Detailed Profiles of Each Record Extreme





🌡️ All-Time High Temperature: 98.0°F


August 11, 2023 • 10-Year Average High: 83.2°F


During the peak of the 2023 persistent subtropical ridge, temperatures at Tampa International Airport climbed to 98.0°F—nearly 15°F above the 10-year average daily high (83.2°F) and marking the hottest single reading across the entire 10-year observational period. Combined with a dew point near 80°F, heat index values exceeded 115°F.








❄️ All-Time Low Temperature: 29.0°F


December 24, 2022 • 10-Year Average Low: 68.3°F


A historic arctic outbreak drove sub-freezing polar air deep into peninsular Florida on Christmas Eve 2022. KTPA bottomed out at 29.0°F—almost 40°F colder than the typical 10-year average low (68.3°F), recording a hard freeze and setting the coldest temperature of the 2015–2024 decade.








💧 Peak Atmospheric Dew Point: 82.0°F


August 7, 2024 • 10-Year Average Dew Point: 64.2°F


Dew points exceeding 75°F are considered oppressive; on August 7, 2024, deep tropical moisture over Tampa Bay surged the dew point to 82.0°F, nearly 18°F above the 10-year baseline average (64.2°F). This saturated atmosphere trapped heat at ground level and delivered record atmospheric moisture content.








🌪️ Lowest Barometric Pressure: 28.69 inHg


September 10, 2017 • 10-Year Average Pressure: 30.04 inHg


As Hurricane Irma tracked northward through the Florida peninsula, its central core induced a dramatic atmospheric pressure collapse. KTPA’s barometer plummeted from its typical 30.04 inHg baseline down to 28.69 inHg (971.5 hPa), the lowest barometric pressure recorded in the 10-year period.








💨 Peak Sustained Wind: 47.0 mph


September 10, 2017 • 10-Year Average Peak Wind: 13.5 mph


The strongest 2-minute sustained wind speed recorded across the 10-year period reached 47.0 mph during Hurricane Irma’s closest approach—more than triple the typical daily peak sustained wind (13.5 mph), accompanied by peak instantaneous wind gusts of 66 mph at airport anemometers.








🌧️ All-Time Wettest Day: 16.14 Inches


August 4, 2024 • 10-Year Average Daily Rain: 0.36 in


Slow-moving tropical moisture feeder bands associated with Hurricane Debby dropped an astounding 16.14 inches of rain in a single 24-hour observational cycle at KTPA—nearly 45 times the typical daily rainfall (0.36 in), shattering all previous 10-year daily rainfall records.

title: Hurricane Idalia (2023)
text:
Synoptic Evolution & Gulf Acceleration
In late August 2023, Hurricane Idalia rapidly intensified over exceptionally warm eastern Gulf waters, ballooning into a Category 4 major hurricane before making landfall in Florida’s Big Bend as a Category 3 storm on August 30.
Although Idalia tracked roughly 120 miles west of Tampa Bay, its eastern flank unleashed persistent southerly and southwesterly gales that pushed Gulf water directly into the mouth of Tampa Bay. Crucially, the surge arrived precisely during an astronomical King Tide (supermoon peak).

title: Hurricane Idalia (2023)
text:
Meteorological Telemetry at KTPA
KTPA’s telemetry documented the dynamics of a high-tide surge disaster:

Pressure & Wind Signature: Station pressure fell to 29.55 inHg on August 30, with sustained onshore winds of 33 mph and squall gusts over 50 mph driving ocean water inland.
Unprecedented Coastal Inundation: The combined astronomical King Tide and 4 to 5 foot surge pushed Tampa Bay to its highest water level since 1993 at the time. Water completely submerged Bayshore Boulevard, flowed through ground-floor condominiums on Davis Islands, and cut off access to Gulf beach communities in St. Petersburg and Clearwater.
Rainfall Total: Outer bands dropped 2.68 inches of rain at KTPA, while the primary damage was caused by saltwater flooding.

title: Hurricane Debby (2024)
section: Synoptic Evolution: The Tropical Moisture Conveyor
text:
Synoptic Evolution: The Tropical Moisture Conveyor
On August 4, 2024, Tropical Storm Debby intensified into a Category 1 hurricane in the northeastern Gulf before making landfall near Steinhatchee. Because Debby was a sprawling, slow-moving system, its eastern circulation tapped into an atmospheric river of deep equatorial moisture.
This persistent moisture train stalled directly over west-central Florida, setting up stationary training thunderstorms that poured unprecedented deluges over Hillsborough and Pinellas counties.

title: Hurricane Debby (2024)
text:
Meteorological Telemetry at KTPA
Debby broke one of the most significant meteorological records in Tampa’s 10-year archive:

All-Time 10-Year 24-Hour Rainfall Record: Over a single 24-hour observation window on August 4, KTPA recorded a staggering 16.14 inches of rain—more than doubling any previous single-day rainfall event in the modern archive.
Extreme Urban and River Flooding: The torrent overwhelmed stormwater drainage across Tampa, flooding major interstates and driving the Hillsborough, Alafia, and Little Manatee rivers into major flood stages that lasted for over a week.
Pressure and Wind Profile: Station pressure dipped to 29.70 inHg with sustained winds reaching 29 mph, demonstrating that rain devastation can vastly outpace wind hazard in slow-moving tropical systems.

title: Anatomy of a Storm
text:
METEOROLOGICAL CASE STUDY


STATION: KTPA • 72-HOUR HURRICANE IRMA TELEMETRY BREAKDOWN

title: Anatomy of a Storm
section: What Happens When a Hurricane Strikes Tampa?
text:
What Happens When a Hurricane Strikes Tampa?
In our 10-year meteorological record of Tampa International Airport (KTPA), one anomaly stands above all others: the early morning hours of September 11, 2017. As Hurricane Irma tore northward up the Florida peninsula, the airport’s automated sensors recorded the violent physical signature of a tropical cyclone passing just miles to the east. By examining hourly barometric pressure, sustained wind speed, and precipitation together across this 72-hour window, we can observe the exact mechanics of what happens when a tropical cyclone strikes Tampa Bay.








Figure 1: Hourly meteorological telemetry recorded at Tampa International Airport (KTPA) during the 72-hour passage of Hurricane Irma (September 9–12, 2017). Top: Station barometric pressure (inHg). Middle: Sustained wind speed (mph). Bottom: Hourly precipitation (inches).






The Barometric Engine
Under ordinary conditions, atmospheric pressure across Tampa Bay hovers around a stable 30.10 inHg (1,019 hPa). As Irma’s circulation approached the Florida Keys on September 9, KTPA’s barometer began a steady, steep descent. By 2:00 AM on September 11, the barometer plummeted to a decade-low record of 28.69 inHg (971.5 hPa). This precipitous V-shaped drop created a steep pressure gradient across western Florida, essentially turning the skies above Tampa into a giant atmospheric siphon that drew in gale-force winds from hundreds of miles away.


Wind and Rain in Lockstep
The middle and bottom panels reveal how closely winds and rainfall sync with barometric collapse. As the pressure bottomed out during the early hours of September 11, sustained winds surged from calm 5–10 mph sea breezes into tropical storm-force gales of 41 to 46 mph, with violent squall gusts recorded up to 66 mph. Simultaneously, heavy spiral rain bands dumped torrential precipitation over Hillsborough County, dropping over 4.5 inches of rain in just a few concentrated hours before the storm center moved north toward Georgia.


The Broader Lesson: Why Storm Track Dictates Tampa Bay’s Fate
What makes Hurricane Irma’s signature particularly revealing is how track geography dictates Tampa Bay’s vulnerability. Because Irma tracked just inland to the east of Tampa, the storm’s counterclockwise rotation drove surface winds out of the northeast and east. These offshore winds pushed bay water outward into the Gulf of Mexico, causing a dramatic “negative storm surge” that temporarily drained the bay floor instead of flooding coastal neighborhoods.
By contrast, when Hurricane Helene (September 2024) passed offshore in the Gulf to the west, and Hurricane Milton (October 2024) made landfall just south near Siesta Key, their counterclockwise winds blew onshore into Tampa Bay. That onshore push, combined with historic rainfall (Milton dumped 16.03 inches at KTPA), transformed that same atmospheric pressure collapse into devastating coastal storm surge. The data confirms that while barometric drop dictates storm intensity, it is the storm’s track relative to Tampa Bay that determines whether water is drained away or driven ashore.

title: Natural Disasters
text:
Chronological Disaster Profiles





🌀 Hurricane Hermine


September 2, 2016 • Category 1 Hurricane


Hermine ended an 11-year hurricane landfall drought in Florida. Its outer circulation drove persistent tropical gale gusts and significant coastal inundation across southern Tampa Bay and coastal Pinellas County.

Explore Full Case Study →







🌪️ Hurricane Irma


September 10, 2017 • Category 4 Hurricane


Irma tracked directly up the spine of the Florida peninsula, triggering the lowest barometric pressure reading of the entire 10-year period (28.69 inHg), sustained winds of 47 mph with gusts to 66 mph, and 11.7 inches of rain.

Explore Full Case Study →







🌊 Hurricane Michael


October 10, 2018 • Category 5 Hurricane


While Michael made landfall in the Florida Panhandle as a monstrous Category 5 storm, its massive counter-clockwise wind field pulled water straight out of Tampa Bay and Hillsborough Bay, creating a rare “reverse negative storm surge.”

Explore Full Case Study →







💨 Hurricane Ian


September 28, 2022 • Category 4/5 Hurricane


Ian initially headed toward Tampa before turning into Cayo Costa. Powerful offshore winds completely drained Tampa Bay’s seabed hours before shifting winds brought dangerous tropical storm-force gusts across the bay area.

Explore Full Case Study →







❄️ Christmas Arctic Freeze


December 24, 2022 • Historic Polar Outbreak


A historic continent-wide polar blast surged sub-freezing arctic air across peninsular Florida on Christmas Eve. KTPA recorded a decade-record low of 29.0°F, bringing a prolonged hard freeze to agricultural and coastal zones.

Explore Full Case Study →







🌊 Hurricane Idalia


August 30, 2023 • Category 3 Hurricane


Passing offshore through the eastern Gulf, Idalia’s storm surge coincided precisely with astronomical high tide, driving unprecedented coastal flooding along Bayshore Boulevard, Davis Islands, and Gulf beaches.

Explore Full Case Study →







🌧️ Hurricane Debby


August 4, 2024 • Category 1 / Tropical Deluge


Debby produced the wettest 24 hours in modern Tampa history. Slow-moving moisture conveyor bands dumped 16.14 inches of rain at KTPA in a single day, causing extensive metropolitan and river basin flooding.

Explore Full Case Study →







🌊 Hurricane Helene


September 26, 2024 • Category 4 Hurricane


Despite tracking over 100 miles offshore, Helene’s immense wind field produced a historic, catastrophic 6–7 ft storm surge that submerged coastal Tampa Bay barrier islands and low-lying coastal neighborhoods.

Explore Full Case Study →







🌀 Hurricane Milton


October 9, 2024 • Category 3 Direct Strike


Just two weeks after Helene, Hurricane Milton made direct landfall near Siesta Key/Tampa Bay. It delivered a 16.03-inch extreme rainfall deluge, an eyewall barometric pressure dip, and hurricane-force wind gusts that tore the roof off Tropicana Field.

Explore Full Case Study →
